The question is not "AI or no AI." It is where to automate, what to protect, and where to collaborate.

Automate · Protect · Collaborate

The three verbs. Say them once here and once at the end.

Research and teaching now sort into three spaces, and each has its own rule.

The map for the rest of the talk. Part one walks the three spaces. Part two stays at the workbench.

Part one
Allocating cognitive work
automate, protect, collaborate

Ten minutes for Part one.

Automate the work that gains nothing from your attention.
  • Planning and tracking
    An append-only handoff file records every session's decisions, so nothing lives only in an agent's memory.
  • Naming and filing
    A drive of 14,238 scanned files became 438 catalogued volumes under one naming scheme.
  • Clerical
    662 dictations, 54,796 words in one month, each cleaned by a model, for about eight dollars.
  • Formatting
    One Markdown feedback letter builds to PDF and Word in a single command.
  • Conversion
    Every PDF a project cites becomes a Markdown file that the checks can read.
  • Routine checks
    Citations and numbers are verified at every commit, before any model reads a word.

Each row is something I actually do. Pick two to say aloud.

The claim is not that the machine can do these. It is that they are poor uses of scarce attention.

The trace: a plain-text log, a diff, a gate receipt. Automation you cannot audit is not automation.

Protect the work through which expertise is built.
  • Reading
    The source, not the summary. A summary cannot tell you what it left out.
  • First ideas
    The question and the hunch, before any model has framed them for you.
  • Learning a procedure
    Running the estimator by hand once, so you can tell when it is wrong later.
  • Some writing
    The first draft of an argument. Originating a claim is a different skill from revising one a machine drafted.
  • Some coding
    Enough to read a change to your code and know what it did to your data.
  • In-class assessment
    The exam, the presentation, the seminar answer given without a prompt window.
  • Oral reasoning
    Defending a claim in real time, which no text model can do for you.

Same form as the automate ledger on purpose. The rows differ in kind, not in difficulty.

Whether the machine can do the task is the wrong test.
The question is not whether the machine can do the task. It is whether you must do it to become able to judge the machine.

What I can offload after twenty years is what a student still has to struggle through.

The student and professor distinction. Kremer's O-ring in one sentence if there is time.

"Human in the loop" says nothing. Say who holds epistemic responsibility.
Collaboration, defined

The human retains epistemic responsibility while the machine changes the scale, speed, or form of what can be done.

Responsibility is the word. Scale, speed, or form is what the machine changes.

Inside the workbench, the working mode follows complexity and verifiability.
Kenny 2026, adapting Swaney 2026. Complexity is how hard the task is. Verifiability is how objectively its output can be checked.

Walk the four cells clockwise from top left. Credit Kenny and Swaney aloud.

Before the grid, a gate: does doing it build the judgment needed to check it?

Kenny's grid sorts how to delegate. The gate asks whether you should.

The riff. His grid sorts delegation; the gate adds the case where you do not delegate.

Research raises the bar. The author certifies correctness.

Software

Goal: a product that works.

Mistakes: usually patched in the next release.

Understanding: no one person needs all of it.

Research

Goal: to know why or how something works.

Mistakes: found before publication, not after.

Understanding: the authors vouch for all of it.

So the workbench needs an audit trail.
After Kenny 2026.

The familiar scholarly problem before any machinery.

A knowledge base connects them. Under each citation sits the source text, or a marked synopsis where the text is not held.
The synopsis layer follows Karpathy 2026's LLM wiki (raw sources, model-written pages, a periodic lint), as in Kenny 2026's demonstration. Here it sits on the verbatim layer, never in its place.

Build it bottom up. The verbatim layer is the point; the wiki sits on it.

Ask the corpus, not the model.
What do my sources say about ethnic and civic conceptions of the nation?
Kohn 1955 gives the classic statement of the dichotomy: membership by political principle versus by descent. synopsis · SOURCES_SYNOPSES.md §1
Tamir 2019 argues the boundary is blurred and that "civic" often exempts a nationalism from scrutiny. full text held
Kohn 1955 · one entry in the synopsis index
Establishes
Originates the influential dichotomy between a Western, rational, voluntarist-political (civic) nationalism and an Eastern, organic, cultural-ethnic nationalism.
Boundary
A foundational historical-typological essay. The West/East geography of the binary is widely critiqued as overdrawn.
Supports
The civic conception centered on shared political principles and citizenship.
The answer cites files, not memory, and marks each source as synopsis or full text.

Captured from the political-regimes project. The answer cites files, and the right panel is one of them.

Now check whether the manuscript says what the source says.
/oss:fact-check manuscript.md
✓ Supported
"a modest, short-lived increase in youth turnout that fades within two election cycles"
Source, lindqvist2019: "modest, on the order of three to four points, and it does not survive beyond the second election."
∼ Partial
"Higher social trust causes higher turnout"
Source, osei2020: "We document an association, not a mechanism." Suggested: is associated with.
✗ Contradicted
"compulsory voting also raises citizens' political knowledge"
Source, ferreira-nair2021: "Whatever compulsory voting does, it does not appear to teach."
A sample project with planted errors, public on the AI for Research site. Every reference passes the format checks. Only reading the source catches the reversal.

The synthetic project from the site's demos. Then the real one, in one sentence: the source cited twice.

Scripts first, at every commit. The model reads last. Whatever was not checked is reported as NOT CHECKED.

Deterministic before generative. The cheap checks run at every commit; the model reads last.

Most of the talk about generative AI is about generation. The useful direction runs the other way.
I am increasingly interested in the opposite direction: using these systems to inspect, retrieve, verify, and challenge what I have written.

The machine is not producing prose. It is keeping an audit trail.

Without ground truth we cannot measure accuracy. We can measure disagreement, and it is a warning.

When transcription error tracks language, it can pass for a cross-national difference in content.

Character-level disagreement among the six best-agreeing systems on body-text pages, from a 64-page, nine-system comparison. Preliminary. No human ground truth exists for this corpus, by a recorded decision.

Say "cross-model agreement", never a character error rate. There is no ground truth by decision.

The corpus that already exists and what it showed. Observational, not causal.

The identity terms in the textbooks do not shift detectably at democratization in 1987.
The pattern

Their character follows regime type and their timing follows curriculum reform, in 1992 to 1997 and again in 2002.

Sixty-seven textbooks. A term counts only when three of four open models agree. Observational, not causal.

The allocation differs for students and for professors.

Students

Automate the clerical.

Protect reading, first ideas, and the procedures you are still learning.

Collaborate only where you can check the output.

Professors

Automate more of your machinery, and leave a trace.

Protect the formation of your students' judgment.

Collaborate: redesign the process around what is now feasible.

Which work we keep, which we hand over, and where new combinations make the impractical practical.

One wiki per piece of research, one manifest per deliverable. The gate is a script that runs at every commit. Lint is a model review that runs only after the gate passes. This deck was built through it.

Appendix. Two commands install the skills.
claude plugin marketplace add scdenney/open-science-skills
claude plugin install oss@open-science-skills

Then name a skill, such as /oss:fact-check, or describe the task and let the matching skill load.
